Q577890.summary: Scratched into the plaster of a room on the Palatine Hill, this crude drawing shows a figure with a donkey's head fixed to a cross, while a young man at left raises a hand in a gesture of worship; the Greek caption beneath reads roughly 'Alexamenos worships [his] god'. It was made to mock a Christian, yet it is among the earliest surviving images of the crucifixion and is often called the oldest known depiction of Jesus. Its very scorn bears witness to how strange the worship of a crucified Lord appeared to the pagan world.
facts: The graffito was discovered in 1857 in a building on the Palatine (the domus Gelotiana) that was later used as a school (paedagogium) for imperial page boys.
In a neighbouring room a different hand wrote 'Alexamenos fidelis' ('Alexamenos is faithful'), which may be a reply to the mockery.
Ancient writers such as Tertullian and Minucius Felix record the slander that Christians worshipped a donkey's head.
Q577890.notes: Dating is disputed (suggestions range from the late 1st to the late 3rd century); Wikipedia gives c. 200 as most likely, while Wikidata records 100. This is a hostile caricature, not a devotional image, and should be presented as such. The photograph is reproduced from Lanciani's 1898 book.
